$doc: Cases shared by the two strip-ansi implementations: crates/veyyon-shell/src/minimizer/primitives.rs (strip_ansi) and packages/utils/src/strip-ansi.ts (stripAnsi).

One corpus because the two used to disagree, and each disagreement was a real defect rather than a stylistic difference: the Rust half stripped CSI only, so an OSC hyperlink kept its body as visible text in minimized shell output; the TypeScript half read parameter bytes as [0-9;?] rather than the spec's 0x30-0x3f, so a colon-subparameter SGR survived; and the TypeScript half kept a stray escape, which is not a fixed point (see escape_run_settles_in_one_pass).

The contract: remove every well-formed sequence, in four grammars. CSI is ESC [, parameter bytes 0x30-0x3f, intermediate bytes 0x20-0x2f, one final byte 0x40-0x7e. A string sequence is ESC and one of ] P X ^ _, a body holding neither BEL nor ESC, then BEL or ST (which is ESC backslash). nF is ESC, one or more intermediate bytes 0x20-0x2f, one final byte 0x30-0x7e. The short class is ESC and one byte in 0x30-0x7e that is not one of those six introducers, which covers Fp, Fe and Fs. An escape that opens none of them is dropped, alone, and the text after it is kept. Nothing else changes, line endings included.
Both test suites read this file and assert exact equality plus idempotence for every case. Add a case here, not in one language.

cases.name: sgr_color
cases.why: The everyday case: a colored word from any build tool.

cases.name: csi_cursor_and_erase
cases.why: Progress rendering is cursor movement and erase, not color, and it is the bulk of what a captured spinner contains.

cases.name: csi_colon_subparameters
cases.why: A true-color SGR written with colon subparameters, which libvte and several test runners emit. The parameter byte range is 0x30-0x3f, so ':' '<' '=' '>' are parameters too; a class of only [0-9;?] leaves 38:2:255:0:0m behind as visible text.

cases.name: csi_private_mode
cases.why: Hiding and showing the cursor, which every interactive tool does on entry and exit.

cases.name: csi_intermediate_byte
cases.why: A sequence with an intermediate byte (0x20-0x2f) between parameters and the final byte: cursor-shape selection.

cases.name: osc_window_title_bel
cases.why: A window-title set terminated by BEL. Shells and test runners write these constantly, and with no OSC handling the escape was dropped and '0;window title' stayed as visible text.

cases.name: osc_hyperlink_st
cases.why: An OSC 8 hyperlink terminated by ST. Emitted by ls --hyperlink, cargo and clang, so this reaches the minimizer from ordinary builds.

cases.name: osc_body_holds_utf8
cases.why: An OSC body is arbitrary text, including multi-byte characters. Both terminators are ASCII, so a scan that ends on one never lands inside a character.

cases.name: osc_unterminated_is_not_a_sequence
cases.why: A capture cut at a buffer boundary mid-OSC has no terminator. The escape byte goes and the rest is kept as text: deleting to the end of the buffer would lose everything after it, which is the failure the CSI half was fixed for.

cases.name: osc_body_broken_by_an_escape_that_is_not_st
cases.why: An ESC inside an OSC body ends the sequence only as part of ST. Here it opens a real CSI instead, so the OSC never completes and the CSI still goes.

cases.name: csi_truncated_keeps_its_tail
cases.why: The regression the CSI scanner exists for: a truncated escape used to delete the whole tail of the capture.

cases.name: fs_independent_control_is_a_sequence
cases.why: ESC b is EMI, one of the independent controls in the Fs class (0x60-0x7e), so a terminal consumes both bytes and draws nothing. This case used to expect 'ab' -- the two-byte grammar was missing, so the letter looked like text that a stray escape happened to precede. The width engine in crates/veyyon-text has always charged zero columns for it, and one of the two had to be wrong.

cases.name: lone_escape_at_end_of_input_is_dropped
cases.why: An escape with nothing after it is the buffer-boundary cut, and it is the case the dropped-escape rule exists for: it renders as nothing, so dropping the one byte costs the operator nothing, and it is what makes a pass a fixed point.

cases.name: escape_before_a_control_byte_is_dropped_alone
cases.why: A newline is outside every introducer and every final-byte class, so this opens no sequence at all: the escape drops alone and the newline survives. Consuming two bytes here would eat a line ending, which is the one thing this function must never change.

cases.name: escape_run_settles_in_one_pass
cases.why: Found by fuzz/fuzz_targets/minimizer_filters.rs. Keeping a stray escape as text let a removal push it against a following '[' and MAKE a sequence, so the same capture minimized to two different things depending on how many passes it had been through.

cases.name: adjacent_sequences_of_both_kinds
cases.why: Sequences arrive back to back, and a scanner that only restarts on text between them misses the second.

cases.name: line_endings_are_preserved_verbatim
cases.why: Stripping decides which bytes are escapes, never how lines end. Carriage returns are a separate primitive's decision and a strip that ate them would hide a \r-overwritten line.

cases.name: text_outside_sequences_keeps_its_characters
cases.why: Multi-byte characters survive intact: the scan copies characters, not bytes.

cases.name: bell_alone_is_not_an_escape_sequence
cases.why: BEL terminates an OSC; on its own it is data. Stripping it would edit output no terminal treats as an escape.

cases.name: plain_text_is_returned_unchanged
cases.why: The fast path. Most captured lines hold no escape at all, and they must come back byte for byte.

cases.name: fp_cursor_save_and_restore
cases.why: ESC 7 and ESC 8 are the two-byte private (Fp) sequences every progress bar uses to park and reclaim the cursor. Neither implementation knew the class, so the escape was dropped alone and the FINAL BYTE stayed as text: a captured spinner handed the model '7done8'.

cases.name: fp_keypad_mode
cases.why: ESC = and ESC > bracket every ncurses application's run, so they arrive on either side of the output an operator actually wanted. Same class as the two above; they left '=' and '>' behind.

cases.name: fs_full_reset
cases.why: ESC c is RIS, which `reset` and `tput reset` emit, and ESC M is reverse index. Both are two-byte Fe/Fs sequences and both used to leave their letter in the text, which reads as a typo in a word rather than as terminal control.

cases.name: nf_charset_selection
cases.why: ESC ( B selects the ASCII charset and is emitted by vim, less and reset. It is ESC plus an intermediate byte plus a final byte, a third grammar again, and it used to leave '(B' in front of the first real word of the output.

cases.name: dcs_payload_is_not_text
cases.why: A DCS string (ESC P, body, ST) carries tmux passthrough and sixel image data. Dropping the escape alone published the whole payload as visible text, which is the OSC-hyperlink defect again with a larger body: an image is thousands of characters of noise in a capture the model reads.

cases.name: apc_payload_is_not_text
cases.why: APC (ESC _, body, ST) is how kitty ships graphics. Same failure as the DCS case, and it is the other string introducer, so the pair proves the family rather than one member of it.

cases.name: string_sequence_terminated_by_bel
cases.why: Terminals accept BEL as well as ST for a string sequence, and programs use both, exactly as they do for OSC.

cases.name: unterminated_string_sequence_keeps_its_tail
cases.why: The truncation rule the CSI and OSC halves already follow: a capture cut inside a DCS has no terminator, so this is not a sequence, the escape is dropped alone and every byte after it survives. Deleting to end of input would silently eat real output at a buffer boundary.

cases.name: csi_and_osc_introducers_are_not_two_byte_sequences
cases.why: The two-byte class covers 0x30-0x7e, which contains '[' and ']'. Matching them there would consume the introducer of a CSI or an OSC and publish its parameters as text, so the class must exclude them and the string introducers. A well-formed CSI directly against a well-formed OSC proves the exclusion holds.

cases.name: two_byte_sequence_run_settles_in_one_pass
cases.why: Idempotence for the new families. ESC ESC 7 is a stray escape followed by a complete Fp sequence: the stray drops, the sequence goes whole, and a second pass cannot find an escape to make a different answer out of.
